title: NovaBio — About Us
content:
NovaBio is a computational drug discovery company leveraging AI-powered molecular simulation to accelerate the journey from target identification to lead optimization. Founded in 2024 by Dr. Wei Zhang and Dr. Sarah Park, we are building the next generation of physics-informed machine learning models that predict molecular behavior with unprecedented accuracy.

Our platform combines quantum mechanical simulations with deep learning to model protein-ligand interactions at atomic resolution. Unlike traditional high-throughput screening approaches that test millions of compounds in the lab, NovaBio's simulations evaluate billions of candidate molecules computationally — reducing discovery timelines from years to months and cutting early-stage R&D costs by an order of magnitude.

Dr. Zhang, a faculty member at MIT and published author in Nature Computational Biology, leads our scientific vision. Dr. Park brings deep industry experience from her tenure at Recursion Pharmaceuticals, where she led the ML infrastructure team responsible for scaling computational pipelines across therapeutic areas.

Based in Boston's Kendall Square, our team of 25 scientists and engineers spans computational chemistry, structural biology, and machine learning. We are currently focused on oncology and rare disease programs, with two internal discovery programs in preclinical stages.

NovaBio is backed by a16z Bio and is committed to making drug discovery faster, cheaper, and more predictable through the power of AI simulation.

title: NovaBio's AI Molecular Simulations Show Promise in Early Drug Discovery
author: Rebecca Torres
content:
A Boston-based startup is making waves in computational drug discovery with a platform that combines physics-based molecular simulation and deep learning to predict drug-target interactions with what the company claims is near-experimental accuracy.

NovaBio, founded in 2024 by MIT computational biologist Dr. Wei Zhang and former Recursion Pharmaceuticals engineer Dr. Sarah Park, published results last month in Nature Computational Biology demonstrating that its AI-driven molecular dynamics simulations could predict binding affinities for a panel of kinase inhibitors with a Pearson correlation of 0.91 against experimental data — a significant improvement over existing computational methods, which typically achieve correlations in the 0.6–0.75 range.

The paper, titled 'Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Molecular Dynamics at Scale,' describes a hybrid architecture that embeds quantum mechanical constraints into a transformer-based neural network. The model was trained on a proprietary dataset of over 50 million molecular conformations generated through high-fidelity density functional theory calculations.

'The key insight is that you don't have to choose between physics and machine learning,' said Dr. Zhang in an interview. 'Our models learn the physics rather than approximating around it. That's what gives us the accuracy.'

The approach addresses a persistent bottleneck in drug discovery: the gap between computational predictions and wet-lab results. Traditional docking and molecular dynamics methods are either too coarse to be predictive or too computationally expensive to run at scale. NovaBio claims its platform can evaluate a library of one billion compounds against a novel target in under 72 hours using cloud compute infrastructure.

Industry observers note that the results, while preliminary, are encouraging. 'If these numbers hold up across diverse target classes, it could meaningfully compress the hit-to-lead timeline,' said Dr. James Liu, a professor of pharmaceutical sciences at UCSF who was not involved in the study.

NovaBio currently has two internal discovery programs in oncology and rare disease. The company raised a $5 million seed round from a16z Bio in 2024 and is understood to be in discussions for a Series A of approximately $18 million.

title: a16z Bio Backs NovaBio's $5M Seed Round for AI-Driven Drug Discovery
author: Michael Chen
content:
Andreessen Horowitz's dedicated biology fund has led a $5 million seed round in NovaBio, a newly formed computational drug discovery startup founded by MIT professor Dr. Wei Zhang and Recursion Pharmaceuticals alumna Dr. Sarah Park.

The round, which also included participation from several angel investors with backgrounds in computational biology and pharma, will fund the buildout of NovaBio's AI molecular simulation platform and the hiring of its initial scientific team.

NovaBio's approach centers on what the founders describe as 'physics-informed deep learning' — machine learning models that incorporate fundamental physical laws governing molecular behavior rather than relying purely on statistical pattern matching. The company believes this hybrid approach can deliver more accurate predictions of how drug candidates will interact with biological targets.

'We've been tracking Wei's research for two years,' said Jorge Conde, general partner at a16z Bio. 'The intersection of modern ML architectures with rigorous physics-based modeling is exactly the kind of approach that could unlock a step-change in computational drug discovery. Most AI drug discovery companies are either doing pure ML or pure simulation — NovaBio is doing both, and doing both well.'

Dr. Zhang, who will serve as CEO while maintaining his faculty position at MIT, said the company plans to focus initially on targets where traditional methods have struggled. 'There are entire classes of drug targets — intrinsically disordered proteins, allosteric sites, protein-protein interactions — where existing computational tools fall short. Our platform is designed from the ground up for these hard problems.'

Dr. Park, who serves as CTO, spent four years at Recursion where she built ML infrastructure supporting the company's drug discovery efforts across multiple therapeutic areas. 'Recursion taught me that the biggest bottleneck in AI drug discovery isn't the algorithms — it's the data pipeline and compute infrastructure,' she said. 'We're building NovaBio's platform to scale from day one.'

The company is based in Boston's Kendall Square and plans to grow to approximately 20 employees by mid-2025.

title: Recursion Pharmaceuticals Reports First AI-Discovered Drug Enters Phase II Trials
author: Jonathan Park
content:
Recursion Pharmaceuticals announced Monday that REC-4881, a compound identified and optimized using the company's AI-driven drug discovery platform, has entered Phase II clinical trials for the treatment of familial adenomatous polyposis, a rare genetic condition that predisposes patients to colorectal cancer.

The milestone marks one of the first instances of an AI-discovered therapeutic advancing to mid-stage clinical testing, a threshold that the broader AI drug discovery industry has been racing to reach. While several AI-identified compounds have entered Phase I trials in recent years, the transition to Phase II — which tests efficacy in a larger patient population — is considered a more meaningful validation of the technology.

'This is the moment the industry has been building toward,' said Recursion CEO Chris Gibson. 'Phase II is where you start to see whether the science actually translates. We're confident in the data, and we're confident in the platform that generated it.'

REC-4881 was identified through Recursion's proprietary platform, which uses high-content imaging and machine learning to map cellular biology at scale. The compound targets the MEK pathway and was optimized through a combination of computational modeling and automated chemistry.

The announcement sent Recursion shares up 14% in early trading. Analysts at Morgan Stanley noted that the Phase II entry could serve as a catalyst for the broader AI drug discovery sector, which has faced skepticism from investors amid a dearth of clinical-stage results.

The development is being closely watched by a generation of newer AI drug discovery startups, including Insilico Medicine, Isomorphic Labs, and NovaBio, all of which are building platforms aimed at different stages of the discovery pipeline.

title: Isomorphic Labs Partners with Eli Lilly in $3B AI Drug Discovery Deal
author: Sarah Johnson
content:
Alphabet's AI drug discovery subsidiary Isomorphic Labs has signed a multi-year collaboration with Eli Lilly valued at up to $3 billion, including $150 million in upfront payments, in one of the largest AI drug discovery partnerships to date.

Under the agreement, Isomorphic will apply its AI-driven molecular design platform — built on technology derived from DeepMind's AlphaFold protein structure prediction system — to identify and optimize drug candidates across multiple therapeutic areas, including oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. Lilly will retain exclusive rights to develop and commercialize any resulting drug candidates.

The deal represents the largest financial commitment a major pharmaceutical company has made to an AI-native drug discovery partner, eclipsing previous agreements such as Sanofi's $1.2 billion partnership with Insilico Medicine and AstraZeneca's collaboration with BenevolentAI.

'Isomorphic's approach to molecular design is genuinely differentiated,' said Daniel Skovronsky, Lilly's chief scientific officer. 'Their ability to model molecular interactions from first principles, rather than relying on historical data alone, opens up target classes that have been intractable for traditional computational methods.'

Demis Hassabis, CEO of both DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, described the partnership as validation of the company's thesis that fundamental advances in AI could transform pharmaceutical R&D. 'We've spent years building the scientific foundation. This partnership is about putting that foundation to work on real therapeutic problems at scale.'

The deal has significant implications for the broader AI drug discovery landscape. Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that the total addressable market for AI-assisted drug discovery could reach $50 billion by 2030, driven by increasing pharmaceutical industry investment in computational approaches. The Lilly partnership is expected to accelerate interest from other pharma companies seeking AI partners.

Shares of publicly traded AI drug discovery companies rallied on the news, with Recursion Pharmaceuticals up 8% and Schrödinger up 6% in the session following the announcement.
